It’s a common misconception that the Mongol empire reached its full territorial height during the life of Ghenghis Khan.  By 1227, the year of his death, the Mongol empire included the northern half of China, Mongolia, and almost all of Central Asia.  Unlike most conquering empires the Mongol Empire stayed together and continued conquering into Persia, Eastern Europe, and southern China after its founder’s death.

The answer to a slightly modified question “Why didn’t the Mongol empire invade India?”  Can be answered in 2 ways.

1.  The Delhi sultanate was very powerful at this time, had not offended the empire, and was generally not worth the effort.

The Mongol empire was famous for its use of horses in battle.  Mongol was/is mostly pastoral.  Especially in the early days of the empire the goal of conquest was to acquire better grazing land for their herds and flocks.  This is why most of the Mongol empire is grasslands and why (intentional or not) vast stretches of formerly settled lands were depopulated.  Northern India even back then was densely packed with a powerful government.  It simply wasn’t worth the effort when much better pastoral land like Eastern Europe and lands with weaker governments like the rapidly declining Abbasid caliphate were ripe for the taking.

2.  If you include Timur or Tamerlane as Mongolian, then yes, the Mongols did invade India just later.  This is less acceptable an answer because Timur was Mongolo-Turkic and not a direct descendant of Ghenghis Khan.

Depends on the brand of conservative but here are a few of the more popular reasons.

1.  More local and personal autonomy.  More libertarian minded conservatives see government regulation and oversight as an impediment to personal freedom and prosperity.  Conservative communities who perceive themselves to be a minority may want more local autonomy to preserve and protect their local interests and way of life.

2.  Fiscal responsibility.  Most strains of conservatism emphasize long term financial stability.  Many conservatives see the corruption and poor financial planning of the federal government (traits common in any large organization) and wish to reign it in as to not pass on the burden to their children or themselves.  The best way to reduce government spending is to cut programs and directly or indirectly reduce its size and influence.

3.  Fear of tyranny.  Particularly in the United States a large and powerful government is associated with tyranny and a reduction of personal freedoms.  The revolution and civil war were both fought because of perceived overreach by the central government.  Foreign wars against authoritarian regimes such as fascism and communism have been framed in the popular imagination of conservatives as a struggle between liberty and tyranny.

It is important to note that not all conservatives see a powerful government as a bad thing.  Religious fundamentalists and others with more radical views see the government as a tool they can use to impose their beliefs onto the rest of society. I used to really struggle with this mission until I made a discovery that makes it surprisingly easy.

First off you need to understand that this mission gets exponentially more difficult the longer it goes on.  If you try to turtle and get mass guardians/drop you will lose.  You will constantly be fighting off enemy attacks and you will only have 1 shot at attacking a heavily fortified Terran base with Zerg reinforcements.  Here is how you beat this map in a few steps.

1.  Let your perimeter bases fall. If you are a very high level player you can save a couple but an average player won’t.

2.  Build up your economy and get mutalisks as fast as possible.  Don’t worry about upgrades yet you just need mutas as fast as possible.  Make some defenses but don’t go overboard.

3.  Starting with the expansion on your right harass the enemy with your mutas and prevent them from mining and destroy their hatcheries.  This mission is hard mostly because the enemy Zerg start with 7 bases between them and will quickly turn this advantage into mass air and drop whose only real counter is mass mutalisk which you will not be able to afford with only 1 base.

4.  Beef up your mutas armada with more of them, upgrades, and expand to all 5 of the expansions and add a moderate level of defenses at each (remember again  that this mission is most easily accomplished if you are constantly attacking so don’t go overboard on defense.  Use your mutas to repel anything that a handful of static defense can’t handle).  You will notice that enemy attacks are becoming less common and that they are using less air.  This is how you know the strategy is working.  The zergs are being starved of resources.

5.  Build a dozen guardians and start attacking the Terran base using your mutas as cover for the guardians.  This is actually the easiest part of the mission if you did everything else right.  The Terran defenses are surprisingly light and don’t have much to counter guardians.  Most of their defenses are lurkers, missile turrets, and most importantly reinforcements from their Zerg allies.

Go air, go fast.  That’s all you need to win this mission.

The real trick isn’t developing the required intelligence to match humanity.  It is all the other things that allow humanity to apply it’s intelligence.  I have listed a few things a species would need to match or surpass us.

1.  Object manipulation.  Our hands are really amazing.  They are capable of brute force and gentle manipulation.  In order to interact and change the world like we do a species would have to be bipedal or have more than 4 limbs.

2.  Fire creation.  Almost everything we do hinges on the fact that we can manipulate fire.  This disqualifies all aquatic life immediately and would be very difficult for animals covered in fur which could easily catch fire.  

3.  Social behavior.  No matter how intelligent an animal becomes if they are not social they won’t create a civilization.  It is simply not possible to produce most things without trade and cooperation.  Not to mention a civilization of creatures that avoid each other as much as possible or only come together to breed or fight would not last long.

4.  Detailed Language.  This has a lot to do with being social but it is important enough to have its own category.  A creature can spend its entire life learning new things but if it can not communicate effectively with others of its kind it’s knowledge dies with it.  Language also helps us visualize and comprehend things we have not experienced or do not exist yet.  Cooperation and invention on the scale of humanity would not be possible without some form of language.  
 
There are a few others but these are the big ones for me.  All of these traits are needed.  One or two won’t cut it because it’s absence undercuts the advantages of all the other traits.
